levels.title: Lighthouse Keeper's Toolkit
levels.story: The lighthouse keeper's tool shed is a mess, and every islander needs a different way to store things. Kit has to match each islander with the right tool, then help run a busy evening shift.

play.needsIntro: Each islander has a job to do. Pick the structure that makes their most common job quick.

needs.need: I want an undo button that always reverses my latest brush stroke first.
hints: The newest stroke has to come back out first.
Last in, first out is a stack.
needs.explain: A stack hands back the newest item first: perfect for undo.

needs.need: Whoever joined the ferry line first should board first.
hints: The person who has waited longest goes next.
First in, first out is a queue.
needs.explain: A queue serves the oldest item first: fair for a line.

needs.need: I need to jump straight to entry number 500 in my tide log, many times a day.
hints: The key job is jumping to a numbered position.
Only one of these reaches any position in a single step.
needs.explain: An array finds any numbered item in one step, because items sit side by side.

needs.need: In a long conga line, I keep adding and removing dancers right next to where I'm standing, without shuffling everyone else along.
hints: Inserting in an array means shifting everything after the gap.
When you're already at the spot, a linked list just relinks two pointers.
needs.explain: In a linked list, adding or removing next to where you are only changes a couple of links.

needs.need: Print the documents in the order people sent them.
hints: The first document sent should come out first.
That's first in, first out.
needs.explain: Print jobs wait in a queue, so they come out in the order they arrived.

play.stackIntro: Crates get stacked on the pier as boats arrive. Watch each push, and predict which crate comes off at each pop.
play.queueIntro: Passengers join the ferry line. Watch each one join, and predict who boards at each dequeue.

words.enqueue: {v} joins the back of the line.
popHints: A stack only lets you reach one end.
It's the crate pushed most recently, the one on top.
dequeueHints: A queue serves whoever has waited longest.
It's the passenger at the front of the line.

feed.prompt: Push A, push B, push C, then pop. What comes off?
feed.explain: A stack gives back the newest item first, and C went on last.

feed.prompt: Enqueue A, B, C. Dequeue twice. Who is still waiting?
feed.answer: Just C. A and B were first in, so they were first out.

feed.prompt: Why is reaching item 500 slow in a linked list, but quick in an array?

options.text: A linked list only knows where the next item is, so you walk there one link at a time
Linked lists store their items in random order
Linked lists can only hold 499 items

feed.explain: Array items sit side by side, so position 500 can be worked out directly. A list has to follow 499 links to get there.

feed.prompt: Your browser's Back button takes you to the page you visited most recently. Which structure does that behave like?
feed.explain: Most recent first is last in, first out: a stack.

feed.prompt: A stack and a queue are both called "abstract data types". What does "abstract" mean here?
feed.answer: They're defined by their operations (push and pop, or enqueue and dequeue), not by how they're built. Either can be built on an array or a linked list.

fieldNotes.title: Every program runs on a stack
fieldNotes.text: When one function calls another, the computer pushes a note onto the call stack saying where to come back to. When a function finishes, its note is popped. Recursion that never stops keeps pushing until the stack runs out of room: that's a "stack overflow", the error the famous coding Q&A site is named after.

fieldNotes.title: Queues keep the internet calm
fieldNotes.text: Big apps rarely do everything the moment you tap a button. Uploading a video or sending an order usually drops a job into a message queue, and worker computers take jobs from the front in turn. If there's a sudden rush, the queue just gets longer for a while instead of the whole app crashing.
fieldNotes.verifyNote: General description of message queues; check the wording is fair. The source link is a general data structures text, not about message queues specifically.

summary: You matched each job to the structure that makes it quick: stacks for newest first, queues for oldest first, arrays for jumping to a position, and linked lists for adding and removing where you already are.
Then you ran a stack and a queue by hand, which is exactly how you'll follow algorithms on the rest of the archipelago.

mistake.title: Mixing up stacks and queues
mistake.text: A stack serves the newest item first. A queue serves the oldest item first. When you're unsure, ask: "does whoever has waited longest go next?" If yes, it's a queue.

everyday.scene: You're drawing in an app. You make three brush strokes: a red one, a blue one, then a green one. You press undo and the green stroke disappears. Press undo again and the blue one goes.
everyday.question: How does the app know which stroke to remove first?
everyday.answer: It keeps your strokes in a stack: a pile where you can only add to the top and take from the top. Each new stroke goes on top, and undo takes the top one off, so the newest stroke always comes back first. That rule is called last in, first out.

lessons.title: Two ways to keep a collection
text: Kit's first stop is the tool shed. A data structure is a way of organising data so the jobs you do most often are quick. To choose one, ask: what will I do with this data most?

An array keeps items side by side in numbered slots, starting at 0. Jumping to slot 500 takes one step, because you can work out where it is. But squeezing a new item into the middle means shifting everything after it along by one.

A linked list keeps items anywhere, and each one holds a note, called a pointer, saying where the next one is. Adding an item right where you're standing means changing two notes. But reaching item 500 means following 499 notes from the start.

terms.meaning: A way of organising data so the jobs you do most are quick.
Items stored side by side in numbered slots.
An item's slot number. We count from 0, so the first item is index 0.
Items that each point to the next one.
A note inside an item that says where another item is.

lessons.diagramCaption: An array has numbered slots side by side. A linked list's items point to each other.

predict.prompt: Which is quicker for "jump straight to item 500": an array or a linked list?
predict.answer: An array. You can work out where slot 500 is. A linked list has to walk there one link at a time.

deeper.title: A first peek at cost
text: Computer scientists count steps. An array takes the same number of steps to reach any item, however long it is. A linked list takes more steps the longer it is.
The next level uses this idea of counting steps to compare different methods.

lessons.title: Stacks and queues: rules for a line
text: A stack works like a pile of plates. You push a plate on top, and you pop the top plate off. The last plate you added is the first one you take. That's last in, first out.
A queue works like the ferry line. People enqueue, which means joining the back, and dequeue, which means leaving from the front. Whoever waited longest goes first. That's first in, first out.
Stacks and queues are defined by their rules, not by how they're built. You can build either one from an array or a linked list, which is why they're called abstract data types.

terms.meaning: Push puts an item on top of a stack. Pop takes the top item off.
Enqueue joins the back of a queue. Dequeue lets the front item leave.
A structure described by what you can do with it, not by how it's built.

lessons.diagramCaption: A stack only lets you reach the top. A queue lets items in at the back and out at the front.

predict.prompt: Your browser's Back button takes you to the page you visited most recently. Is that a stack or a queue?
predict.answer: A stack. The most recent page comes off first.

deeper.title: Your programs run on a stack
text: When a function calls another function, the computer pushes a note onto the call stack saying where to come back to. When the function finishes, the note is popped.
Code that keeps calling itself without stopping keeps pushing until the stack runs out of room. That error is called a stack overflow.

lessons.title: Picking the right tool
text: Choosing a data structure is about matching the job to the tool. Newest first? Stack. Fair, oldest first? Queue. Jump straight to a numbered spot? Array. Add or remove items right where you're standing? Linked list.
There is no single best structure. Each one is quick at some jobs and slow at others. Ask what the data will be used for most, then pick.

head: The job
The tool
rows: Add or remove right next to where you are

lessons.diagramCaption: Match the job to the tool.

predict.prompt: A printer must print documents in the order people sent them. Which tool?
predict.answer: A queue: first in, first out.

levels.title: Growth Race
levels.story: It's regatta day at the harbour. Every boat runs on a different formula, and each captain claims their boat has the gentlest climb, staying cheap even as the course gets longer. Kit's job is to find out who's right.

play.rankIntro: Tap the boats from the gentlest climb (slowest-growing) to the steepest.

rankItems.hint: Start with the one that doesn't grow at all.

rankItems.label: log n
rankItems.hint: Next: the one that only grows by one step each time n doubles.

rankItems.label: n
rankItems.hint: Next: the one that grows in step with n.

rankItems.label: n log n
rankItems.hint: Next: a little steeper than n, because of an extra log factor.

rankItems.label: 2ⁿ
rankItems.hint: Last: the one that doubles every time n goes up by just one.

play.rankDone: Gentlest to steepest: 1, log n, n, n log n, n², 2ⁿ.
play.raceIntro: Captain Ada's boat needs 100n steps. Captain Bo's needs n². Fewer steps is better. Predict who's ahead at each marker.
play.raceAsk: At n = {n}, whose boat needs fewer steps?
raceHints: Work out both: multiply n by 100 for Ada, and n by itself for Bo.
At n = {n}, Ada needs {a} steps and Bo needs {b}.
play.raceSay: At n = {n}: Ada needs {a} steps, Bo needs {b}.
play.raceStart: The boats line up. Nobody has moved yet.
play.raceDone: Bo looked better for small n, but n² overtakes 100n from n = 100 on. Small inputs can fool you.
play.countTitle: Count it: find the biggest crate
play.countIntro: The harbour master scans the crates left to right, keeping the biggest one so far. Before running it, predict how many comparisons it takes.
play.countPrompt: How many comparisons to find the biggest of these 8 crates?
countHints: The first crate starts as "biggest so far" without any comparison.
Every other crate is compared once.
play.countSay: Compare {v} with the biggest so far ({m}).
play.countStart: Crate 4 starts as the biggest so far. No comparison needed yet.

follow.prompt: So with n crates, how many comparisons does finding the biggest take?

options.text: n − 1, so the work grows in step with n
n², so the work quadruples when n doubles
log n, so the work barely grows

hints: 8 crates took 7. Guess what 16 crates would take.
Every crate after the first gets one comparison.
follow.explain: n − 1 comparisons: double the crates, double the work. That's linear growth.

challenge.title: Challenge: true or false?
challenge.offer: Bonus round: Captain Ada and Captain Bo make bold claims using the O, Ω and Θ notation from the Go deeper box on the last lesson page. It's optional, and mistakes here never cost you stars.
challenge.intro: Use the f(n)/g(n) ratio test when you're unsure.

hints: Divide by n²: (3n² + 5n)/n² = 3 + 5/n.
That settles on 3, a positive number, so they grow at the same rate.
statements.explain: True. The ratio settles on 3, so it's even Θ(n²), and Θ implies O.

hints: Divide: n²/n = n.
The ratio shoots to infinity, so n² grows faster than n.
statements.explain: False. n² outgrows n, so n can't be an upper bound for it.

hints: O is only an upper bound. It doesn't have to be tight.
n/n² = 1/n goes to 0, so n grows slower than n².
statements.explain: True. An upper bound can be loose: n grows no faster than n².

hints: Changing a log's base only multiplies it by a constant.
log₂ n = log₁₀ n / log₁₀ 2, so the ratio is a constant.
statements.explain: True. All log bases grow at the same rate.

hints: Ω means "grows at least as fast as".
(n log n)/n² = (log n)/n goes to 0, so n log n grows slower.
statements.explain: False. n log n grows slower than n², so n² isn't a lower bound for it.

hints: The ratio is exactly 2, a constant.
statements.explain: True. 2ⁿ⁺¹ is just 2 times 2ⁿ, a constant factor.

feed.prompt: Which grows fastest as n gets huge?
feed.explain: Exponential beats every polynomial in the end: 2ⁿ doubles each time n goes up by one.

feed.prompt: 100n against n²: from which value of n does n² need at least as many steps?
feed.answer: From n = 100. There, both need 10,000 steps. After that, n² pulls ahead fast.

feed.prompt: Why do we drop constants, like the 3 in 3n², when stating growth rates?

options.text: Constants don't change how the cost grows as n gets big

feed.explain: Double the input and 3n² still quadruples, just like n². The constant depends on the machine, while the growth rate depends on the method.

feed.prompt: A method takes n² steps. If n goes from 1,000 to 2,000, how many times more work is that?
Finding the biggest of 1,000 crates by scanning them once: how many comparisons?
feed.answer: 999. Every crate after the first gets one comparison, so n − 1.

feed.prompt: What does log n tell you?

options.text: How many times you can halve n before you reach 1

feed.explain: log n is a halving count. It grows very slowly, which is why halving methods stay cheap.

fieldNotes.title: A billion items: 30 seconds or 30 years
fieldNotes.text: Say a computer does a billion basic steps per second. Sorting a billion items with an n log n method takes about 30 billion steps: around 30 seconds. A method doing n² steps would need a billion billion steps: about 30 years. Same computer, same data, completely different growth rate.
fieldNotes.verifyNote: Check: log₂(10⁹) ≈ 30, so n log n ≈ 3 × 10¹⁰ steps ≈ 30 s at 10⁹ steps/s; n² = 10¹⁸ steps ≈ 10⁹ s ≈ 31.7 years.

fieldNotes.title: The chessboard of rice
fieldNotes.text: An old story: put 1 grain of rice on the first square of a chessboard, 2 on the next, 4 on the next, doubling each time. The total over all 64 squares is 2⁶⁴ − 1, about 18 quintillion grains. That's 2ⁿ growth, and it's why exponential-time algorithms are hopeless for large inputs.

summary: You ranked growth rates, watched n² overtake 100n, and counted the comparisons in a real method. If you tried the challenge, you also judged O, Ω and Θ claims with the ratio test.
Counting steps and then asking "how does this grow as n grows?" is the heart of analysing algorithms. Every island from here on uses it.

mistake.title: Trusting small inputs
mistake.text: At n = 10, Bo's n² boat looked better than Ada's 100n. But growth rate decides the winner once n gets big. Always ask what happens as n grows, not what happens for one small example.

everyday.scene: A small app runs smoothly with 100 users. Then it becomes popular, and with 100,000 users it grinds almost to a halt. Nobody changed the code.
everyday.question: If the code didn't change, why did the app slow down so much?
everyday.answer: What changed was the input size, called n. If the app does about n × n steps, 100 users means 10,000 steps, but 100,000 users means 10 billion. That's a thousand times more users but a million times more work. How fast the work grows as n grows decides whether an app survives its own success.

lessons.title: Count steps, not seconds
text: Kit's first rule for the regatta: don't time boats with a stopwatch, because a faster computer would always win. Instead, count the basic steps a method takes, like comparisons, and write the count in terms of n, the number of items it has to handle.

Example: the harbour master looks for the biggest crate among n crates by scanning left to right and keeping the biggest so far. The first crate needs no comparison, and each of the other crates is compared once. That's n − 1 comparisons. Double the crates and the work doubles.

terms.meaning: A step-by-step method for solving a problem.
How many items the method has to handle.
Checking which of two things is bigger.

lessons.diagramCaption: Scanning for the biggest crate: the work grows in step with n.

predict.prompt: How many comparisons does it take to find the biggest of 100 crates?
predict.answer: 99. Every crate after the first gets one comparison, so n − 1.

lessons.title: Gentle climbs and steep climbs
text: Methods grow at different speeds as n gets bigger. From gentlest to steepest: 1 (constant: it doesn't grow at all), log n, n, n log n, n² and 2ⁿ.

What's a logarithm? log n asks: how many times can you halve n before you reach 1? For 1,000,000 that's only about 20 halvings. So a method that halves the problem at each step stays cheap even for huge inputs.
n² means n × n: double n and the work quadruples. 2ⁿ means 2 multiplied by itself n times: add just 1 to n and the work doubles. That's why 2ⁿ explodes. 2³⁰ is already over a billion.

terms.meaning: How quickly the number of steps grows as n grows.
How many times you can halve n before you reach 1.
The small raised number: n² means n × n.

lessons.diagramCaption: Steps needed as n grows. The 2ⁿ column explodes long before n gets big.

predict.prompt: If n doubles, what happens to the work for a method that takes n steps? And for one that takes n² steps?
predict.answer: The n method takes twice as long. The n² method takes four times as long.

deeper.title: Does the base of a log matter?
text: log₂ n and log₁₀ n differ only by a constant factor, so they grow at the same rate. That's why computer scientists usually write just "log n".

lessons.title: Small inputs can fool you
text: Captain Ada's boat needs 100n steps. Captain Bo's needs n². At n = 10, Bo needs only 100 steps and Ada needs 1,000, so Bo looks brilliant. At n = 100 they tie at 10,000 steps. After that, Bo falls behind fast.

That's why we care about growth as n gets large, not one small example. It's also why multipliers matter less than the shape: 100n and 3n are both "n-shaped", and 3n² + 5n behaves like n² once n is big, because the biggest term takes over.

terms.meaning: A plain number multiplying the steps, like the 100 in 100n.

predict.prompt: At n = 1,000, whose boat needs fewer steps: Ada's 100n or Bo's n²?

deeper.title: O, Ω and Θ, and the ratio test
text: Computer scientists write O(g) for "grows no faster than g" (an upper bound), Ω(g) for "grows at least as fast as g" (a lower bound), and Θ(g) for "grows at the same rate as g".

A handy test: work out f(n)/g(n) as n gets huge. If it goes to 0, f grows slower. If it settles on a positive number, they grow at the same rate. If it shoots to infinity, f grows faster. Example: (3n² + 5n)/n² = 3 + 5/n settles on 3, so 3n² + 5n is Θ(n²).
